questions.what: When a colleague asks what the product is, can the reader answer in one sentence that tells them what it does?
Reading the gain, can the reader tell what the product would let them do, and so whether it is for them?
When a colleague asks why this product and not another way of doing the same work, can the reader name what it does differently that brings the gain?
Before installing, can the reader tell what the product does not do that they might have expected of it?
After the walkthrough, can the reader tell that the product would give them, on work of their own, the gain the opening promised?
Starting with nothing set up, can the reader install the product by the README's steps alone, and tell that it works?
For each gain and the idea, can the reader see in the figure of how the product works how the product keeps it?
When the reader needs more than the README gives, such as fuller use or a change to the product, can they tell from it where to read next?
Can the reader tell from the README the terms on which they and their team may use the product?
Reading from the top, does the reader find each answer just when they come to need it, so they can stop as soon as they have what they came for?

decisions.what: Which name does the README give each thing, and where does the reader learn it?
decisions.decided: A work: what you want made. Its kind: the sort of work it is, such as a README. A point: one thing the work's design must settle, a fact or a decision. These three are defined in the person's gain where first used. The design: the work's purpose with every point settled under it, kept in the design file design-tree.json. A kind's best practice: the parts a good work of the kind has, the questions it answers yes to, and a way to make each yes. The generator and the evaluator: the AI that makes the work and the fresh AI that judges it; these four are defined in the idea. A calling AI: defined in its paragraph. Each keeps one name from start to end, in the figure too. Differs from the old README, which called the best practice a template.

decisions.what: What is Turn, in one sentence?
decisions.decided: Turn is a Claude Code plugin that makes a work you ask for, such as a README or a module of code, ready to use as it comes, and asks you only the decisions that are yours. A colleague who hears only this can say: it makes a document or code that I can use as it comes, and it asks me only my own decisions. Differs from the old summary, whose "until it meets your purpose well" told the colleague nothing they could check.

decisions.what: What does the person gain, and how can a reader tell Turn is not for them?
decisions.decided: For you when you want an AI in Claude Code to make a work you will put to use, such as a README or a module of code, and you would rather answer a few points than read and mend a draft. Turn finds each fact itself, asks you only the decisions that are yours, and hands over the work written in your repository, for you to put to use as it comes. A last sentence tells the reader outside the group: for a quick draft that you would read and fix yourself, Turn takes longer than asking Claude Code alone. Differs from the old gain by that last sentence, moved from the non-goals, and by naming the work's hand-over.

decisions.what: What does the calling AI gain, and how can an AI tell Turn is not for it?
decisions.decided: For you if you are an AI that connects a person and Turn, such as a role of another plugin that carries a larger plan for the person. You hand Turn the work, the points you have settled with the person, and where the work goes. Turn keeps those points as given and does not ask the person them again. You pass each point Turn gives you to the person as given, and the answer back word for word. You get back the work, and pass it on as it is. An AI with no person to answer is outside the group, as a point that is the person's waits for them. Differs from the old README, which said only that the plugin gets back the work.

decisions.what: What does Turn do that another way of doing the same work does not?
decisions.decided: The other way: asking an AI for the work in one prompt, or using an agent that writes the work and checks it itself. The AI fills each gap of the request with a guess, and passes its own work by what it meant to write, so you meet the guesses when you use the work, and mend it. Turn instead settles the work's design with you first, makes the work against the best practice of its kind, has a fresh AI judge it in the place of the one who will use it, and then refines how it reads. Five parts follow, each with what it ensures: a best practice for each kind (a kind new to Turn gets one, its purpose and questions approved by you); the design settled with you first, by Pin; made against the best practice, by the generator; judged by the evaluator, fresh, with the work and the questions only, a question not met taken back to the decision behind it; then refined for how it reads, by the same two with the questions of how a document reads or code is written, what the work says kept. A colleague can say: it agrees the design with me first, and another AI that never saw the design checks the work as its reader would. Differs from the old idea, which named no other way by what it does and kept a part, making parts at once, that brings a shorter wait and not the gain.

decisions.what: What might the reader expect of Turn that it does not do?
decisions.decided: Three, set apart under Non-goals: Turn does not check whether the work gets you what you want of it in the world, such as more users for your tool; Turn does not commit, push or publish the work; Turn does not decide a point that is yours, and a point left unanswered holds the run. The old non-goal of a quick draft moves to the gain (D5), where the reader outside the group meets it.

decisions.what: What does the figure of How it works show, so each gain and the idea can be seen in it?
decisions.decided: An SVG in plugins/turn/images/how-it-works.svg. Outside Turn: you, a calling AI and your repository. Inside Turn, a frame: Pin, the best practices, design-tree.json, the generator, the work and the evaluator, with no other role. Arrows: you to Turn, your request then each answer; Turn to you, one point at a time, the design, then the work (gain of O1); a calling AI between you and Turn, passing each point and answer on as given, handing Turn the points it settled, getting back the work (gain of O2); Pin finds each fact in your repository and writes each point into design-tree.json; the best practices give Pin their questions and the generator how to make each yes; the generator builds on the design and writes the work; the evaluator reads the work whole, its box saying it has the questions only, never the design; a question not met goes back to Pin. The best practices box says the kind's, then how it reads, for the last part of the idea. Differs from the old Mermaid flowchart, which showed six roles, up and Lane's routes.

decisions.what: In what order do the parts stand?
decisions.decided: The summary; the person's gain; the calling AI's gain; the idea with its five parts; Non-goals; Requirements; Installation; Walkthrough; How it works; Documentation; Development; License. Read from the top, each part answers the question the one before leaves: what is it, is it for me, for an AI too, why this way, what it will not do, what I need, how I install it, what a run gives me, how it keeps its promises, where to read more, on what terms.
